triageSets._prefix: Prefix for the full episode (id e14_social_media). The defend-only shell (id e14_social_media_defend) sets episode_e14_social_media_defend_defend_ instead, as E1/E4/E8 do. No stage on purpose, as in E1/E4: the effective stage is 'mission', and an explicit stage with passPercent 0 draws a validator warning.
triageSets._kinds: The engine has no 'DM' or 'connection request' kind (triage-kinds.js NON_EMAIL_KINDS), so every item is a `sms` card (the direct-message surface): from.name is the display name and from.address is the sender handle (e.g. @jordan.vale, not an email). 'DM' / 'connection request' is the in-fiction framing. verifyVerdict is false: the moves are Trust, Report and Delete, with no 'ring a number' item.
triageSets._localTells: fake_profile and recon_request are social-media reconnaissance signs with no built equivalent, so they are scenario-local to this set (00 section 2's CHANNEL_TELLS is untouched, and no SKILL_NAMES entry is added to phish-rules.js/triage.rb). Each is declared in channelTells with a flagChips label and a set-level skillNames name (triage-flags.js reads set.skillNames for a local tell's skill name), and every flagging message carries a factorStrings.<id>.redFlag sentence. Promote one to the shared library only if a 10 check item later scores it. lookalike_domain and secrecy_or_bypass are shared-library tells (offered as chips, no message scores them here, as E4 lists reply_to_differs without using it).
triageSets.title: Messages and requests
triageSets.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Merrin & Sallow Architects, a fictional practice. Six messages and connection requests are waiting. For each one, choose Trust, Report or Delete, then tick what you noticed. The tell is always what they ask for, not how friendly they are. Reporting or checking when you're unsure is always fine and never marked down.

genuineCopy.binnedLeadOne: One real message was treated as a fake
genuineCopy.binnedLeadMany: {n} real messages were treated as fakes
genuineCopy.costBoth: Reporting when you're unsure is never wrong, but a report on a real message takes someone's time to check, and a deleted one leaves a genuine colleague or recruiter waiting.
genuineCopy.costReport: Reporting when you're unsure is never wrong, but a report on a real message takes someone's time to check, and the person waits for a reply.
genuineCopy.costBin: Deleting a real message has a cost: a genuine recruiter or colleague is left waiting for a reply.
genuineCopy.whyBothHalves: Both halves matter: spotting the fake messages protects you and your colleagues, and answering the real ones keeps work and friendships going.

skillNames.fake_profile: Spotting a fake or thin profile
skillNames.recon_request: Spotting a stranger fishing for how your firm works

messages._note: Row 1. The normal-looking phish half of the mirror pair: a tempting recruiter DM from a thin new account that steers straight to the firm's systems and who runs IT. fake_profile + recon_request. Report.
messages.body: [New account, created last week, no other posts.] Hi! Came across your profile, I've a great architecture role that would suit you. To tailor the application, could you send a quick overview of the systems your firm uses and who runs your IT?

fake_profile.redFlag: A new account with a thin history, impersonating someone or inventing a persona

recon_request.redFlag: A stranger asking about your firm's systems, security tools, org chart or who runs IT

perFlagNote.fake_profile: A brand-new account, almost no history, and it moved to the systems question fast: a fake recruiter profile used to scout your firm
perFlagNote.recon_request: A genuine recruiter never needs a breakdown of your firm's systems or who runs IT. That is scouting, not recruitment

truth.ifTrusted: A map of the studio's systems and who runs IT would go to a stranger, ready-made for the next scam.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. There's no such recruiter; the account is a week old. Share nothing about our systems, and report it. This is the normal-looking phish you'll see most.

messages._note: Row 2. A connection request in the managing partner's name from a second, new, thin account (handle @catherine.merrin.2). The look-alike NPC guard flags the duplicate senior name in the full episode; here it carries fake_profile. Catherine's real profile is the established one. Report.
messages.body: [New account, created this week, 3 connections.] Hi, let's connect. Always good to stay close to the team.

fake_profile.redFlag: A new account with a thin history, impersonating someone or inventing a persona

perFlagNote.fake_profile: A second account in the managing partner's name, new and thin, when her real profile is the established one: a fake used to connect to staff and lend weight to a later scam

truth.ifTrusted: Connecting hands a stranger a foothold in the managing partner's name to approach your colleagues.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. Catherine's real profile is the one you already follow; this one is days old. A senior name on a new account is a classic fake. Report it.

messages._note: Row 3. Genuine: a real agency recruiter with a role and no questions about systems. Roseanne Wadsworth at Kettlewick Talent (built genuine agency). Trust; 'report everything' is not the win. Under the awareness profile a genuine item scores full whether Trusted or Reported.
messages.body: A practice I work with is hiring a Part 3 architect, and your profile looks a good fit. Shall I send you the brief?

whyFine.default: A real agency recruiter with a named role and no questions about your systems or who runs IT. Nothing to report; 'report everything' is not the win, and this is the recruiter the fake one is dressed up as.

messages._note: Row 4. A friendly opener on the feed that steers to the studio's tools. recon_request. Report. A genuine-looking account (Elif Demir), which is the point: the ask is the tell, not the account.
messages.body: Loved your bridge model on the feed! Out of interest, what software does the studio run day to day?

recon_request.redFlag: A stranger asking about your firm's systems, security tools, org chart or who runs IT

perFlagNote.recon_request: A friendly opener that steers to the tools the studio runs is still scouting. You don't owe a stranger your firm's systems

truth.ifTrusted: Naming the studio's software hands a stranger the first piece of a convincing cover story.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. The compliment was real enough; the question wasn't their business. Share nothing about our tools with a stranger, and report it.

messages._note: Row 5. Genuine: a colleague you know asking for something ordinary through a normal channel. Thandiwe Moyo (built studio manager). Trust and handle it.
messages.body: Can you send me the studio floor plan for the client visit on Thursday? Ta.

whyFine.default: A colleague you know, asking for something ordinary through a normal channel. Nothing to report; handle it.

messages._note: Row 6. The suspicious-looking genuine half of the mirror pair: a real former colleague, now elsewhere, offering a lead. It reads like a recruiter pitch but asks nothing about systems. Harriet Beaumont. Trust. Pairs with row 1 (fake_recruiter, Report).
messages.body: Good to reconnect! We've a junior role opening here if you fancy it, happy to put your name forward. No pressure either way.

whyFine.default: It reads like a recruiter pitch, but it's a real former colleague offering you a lead and asking nothing about your work. The tell is what they ask for, not how friendly they are. Trusting it is right, and reporting it still scores full.

awarenessEpisode.scopeNote: Authorised exercise at Merrin & Sallow Architects, a fictional practice. In scope: Dani Fenwick's public posts and your own profile. Nothing you do here leaves this room.

strings.teamLine: By reporting {n} of these rather than answering, you kept a fake message away from the rest of your team.
strings.weakestTells: The signs most often missed: {names} ({counts} each).
strings.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Merrin & Sallow Architects, a fictional practice. First you play the attacker's side: look at what one colleague, Dani Fenwick, has posted in public, pin what an attacker would use, then write one short message built from it. Then you swap sides: you spot the same tricks in a feed and an inbox, and close the gaps, on Dani's profile. Only the inbox is scored.
strings.flipIntro: This is the message you just sent, as Yasmin read it while covering for Dani. The lines picked out below are what make it fit the week.
strings.flipDefenderLine: It named Dani's leave, the new system and his manager, and asked for one small thing, all built from public posts. When a message fits the week, a colleague acting on it is the ordinary thing to do.
strings.flipNoSend: Your message didn't go out this time, so there's nothing of yours to show. Next, you spot the same moves in a feed and an inbox, and close the gaps, on Dani's profile.
strings.flipMissed: The defence is the same either way: next, you spot the same moves in a feed and an inbox, and close the gaps, on Dani's profile.
strings.flipLandedNoTells: It read as an ordinary note from a colleague, with nothing in it to question. Next, you spot the same moves in a feed and an inbox, and close the gaps.
strings.allPhishRight: Every fake was caught, with every tell named.
strings.noBlameLine: A convincing profile of a person is built from scraps anyone could find. Nobody is foolish for having posted them; the fix is a setting and a pause, not shame.
strings.defendIntro: Now the inbox: mark each message Trust, Report or Delete, and tick what gave it away. A friendly opener that steers to your firm's systems or who runs IT is still scouting; report it. There's no clock on you here.
strings.mondayCard: On Monday: tighten one privacy setting today, and check what's behind you before your next post or video call. And if a stranger asks about your firm's systems or who runs IT, share nothing and report it using the route in the box below.
strings.defendOnly: A well-made message is built from scraps anyone could find online, and anyone can be pulled in by one. The ones you were caught out by are shown below, with what gave each one away.

_defendOnly.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Merrin & Sallow Architects, a fictional practice. A feed and an inbox are waiting: some posts are fine, some give too much away, and some messages were made to pull work details out of you. Sort them, close the gaps, and report the fakes. Reporting or checking when you're unsure is always fine and never marked down.
